finding.claim: The /checkout route computes the charge from client-supplied item price and qty. An attacker can set the price to 0.01 or a negative number, or qty to a negative number, so the total is near zero or negative. They can then buy items at an arbitrary price, or trigger a negative charge that may act as a refund or credit. The /checkout-v2 route fixes this by looking up prices in the catalog, so the vulnerable route is likely a leftover legacy endpoint that is still mounted.
finding.source: req.body.items[].price and req.body.items[].qty, sent in the JSON body of POST /checkout by any authenticated user
finding.sink: req.payments.charge(req.user.id, total) at cart.js:6 charges the attacker-computed total

trace.note: POST /checkout handler. No validation or catalog lookup in this file.
total = sum of i.price * i.qty, using the attacker's own price and qty values with no type, range or sign checks
The attacker-controlled total is passed to payments.charge
The same total is returned as the charged amount

finding.guards_checked: This file has no server-side price lookup, no qty or price validation (sign, integer, upper bound), and no SKU check on this route. The only other code in the file is /checkout-v2, which does use the catalog price and clamps qty to at least 1 with Math.max(1, Math.floor(qty)). Any auth middleware or validation in the parent app is not in this directory, and none of it can fix the trust in client-supplied price.

verdict.reason: cart.js:5 sums client-supplied i.price * i.qty with no validation or catalog lookup and cart.js:6 charges that total, whereas /checkout-v2 (cart.js:13-14) shows the intended catalog lookup and qty clamp are missing here; any authenticated user (req.user.id) can reach it, and the only unseen controls are parent-app auth, which can't fix price trust.
